title: A 12-Week Training Plan for Kilimanjaro
excerpt: You do not need to be an athlete to climb Kilimanjaro, but training makes the climb more enjoyable. This 12-week plan builds endurance step by step.
body:
The aim of training for Kilimanjaro is simple: be able to walk for six to eight hours on several days in a row, uphill and downhill, while carrying a small daypack.

## Weeks 1–4: build a base

- Three times a week 30–45 minutes of cardio: brisk walking, cycling, swimming or running.
- One longer walk at the weekend of two to three hours.
- Twice a week simple strength work: squats, lunges, step-ups and core exercises.

## Weeks 5–8: add distance and height

- Increase weekday sessions to 45–60 minutes.
- Weekend walks of four to five hours, with as much elevation as you can find: hills, dunes, stairs or a stair machine.
- Start walking with the daypack you will use, with 5–7 kg in it.
- Break in your boots now.

## Weeks 9–11: back-to-back days

- Plan at least two weekends with long walks on both Saturday and Sunday. This simulates consecutive days on the mountain.
- One long session of six hours or more.
- Keep strength training going, focusing on legs and core.

## Week 12: taper

Reduce volume, keep moving lightly, sleep well. Arrive rested.

## Living in a flat country

Most of our travellers come from the Netherlands and Belgium, where hills are scarce. Stairs, stair machines and treadmills on an incline help. A weekend in the Ardennes, the Eifel or the Alps is a great test.

## What training does not do

Training does not protect against altitude sickness. It makes you more comfortable and helps you recover overnight. Days on the mountain still matter most. See [Altitude sickness on Kilimanjaro](/blog/kilimanjaro-altitude-sickness/) and our page on [preparing for Kilimanjaro](/preparing-for-kilimanjaro/).

Check with your doctor before starting a new training programme.
